mkdir -p ~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec05

# `tmux` on the server: keep your work alive

This is what `tmux` from Lecture 2 is for. Start it *on the server*, right after you log in, and run your long job inside it:

```bash
ssh moriah
tmux new -s analysis             # a session on the server
Rscript long_job.R               # start the long job
# Ctrl+B then D : detach
exit                             # log out; the job keeps running
```

Close your laptop, lose your Wi-Fi, go home. Later:

```bash
ssh moriah
tmux ls                          # analysis: 1 windows ...
tmux attach -t analysis          # back where you left off, output and all
```

The session lives on the server, not on your laptop, so it survives a dropped `ssh` connection as well as a deliberate logout.

`nohup` from Lecture 2 also works for this but `tmux` is the safer choice where the job's terminal belongs to the `tmux` session, which never goes away when you log out. Neither one comes with a guarantee. A remote server is not your machine: the system administrator is in control and can kill anything they want. They may set the server to kill all of your processes when you log out, `tmux` included, or kill any job that runs too long or uses too much memory on a shared login machine. Read your server's rules, and on a cluster put long jobs in the "scheduler", which is what it is there for. We will return to the scheduler later (on moriah they use a program called SLURM).

Make it a habit: whenever you `ssh` in to do something that takes more than a minute, start or attach to a `tmux` session first.


# Using Postgres on Moriah

Log into moriah and try `psql`. You will most likely get `command not found`. A cluster serves hundreds of users who need different programs, and often different versions of the same program, so most software is installed side by side and switched off until you ask for it. The `module` command does the asking. First search for what is available:

```bash
ssh -J kapelner@bava.cs.huji.ac.il kapelner@moriah-gw.cs.huji.ac.il
psql #fails
```

This gives

```
psql: error: connection to server at "*" (127.0.0.1), port 5432 failed: Connection refused
        Is the server running on that host and accepting TCP/IP connections?
```

We need to "load" it on the server:

```bash
module spider postgres           # every Postgres version installed here
module spider postgres/17        # details about one version
```

`module spider` only *searches*. To actually use a version, load it:

```bash
module load postgres/17          # adds psql and friends to your PATH
which psql                       # now found
psql --version
```

A loaded module lasts only until you log out, and the next login starts clean again. To load it every time, put the line into `~/.bashrc` on Moriah, which bash runs at the start of every session. Then `source` the file, which runs it in the current shell, so you do not have to log out and back in:

```bash
echo 'module load postgres/17' >> ~/.bashrc   # >> appends; > would wipe the file
source ~/.bashrc
```

From now on Postgres is there every time you log in, and you never need to think about this whole `module` thing ever again.

## More queries



## Continuing with grouped aggregate queries

Review: `GROUP BY` splits the rows into groups, here one group per state, and the aggregate is computed separately for each group, so the answer has one row per group. 


`HAVING` then filters the groups, the way `WHERE` filters the rows: `WHERE` runs before the grouping and `HAVING` after it, so only `HAVING` can test an aggregate such as `count(*) < 5`. The order of the clauses is `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, then `ORDER BY`:


```sql
-- group by two columns: one group per county (county names repeat across states, so state is needed too)
SELECT state, county, max(cases) FROM covid
  GROUP BY state, county ORDER BY max(cases) DESC LIMIT 3;  -- Los Angeles 770915, New York City 430863, Cook 393652
-- HAVING filters the groups, after they are computed (WHERE filters the rows, before)
SELECT state, count(*) FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
  GROUP BY state HAVING count(*) < 5 ORDER BY count(*);     -- District of Columbia 1, Guam 1, Northern Mariana Islands 2, Virgin Islands 3, Delaware 4
```

There is one rule to remember. Every column after `SELECT` must either be in the `GROUP BY` or be inside an aggregate. `SELECT state, county, count(*) ... GROUP BY state` fails, because a state has many counties and Postgres cannot know which one to show. (A `GROUP BY` with no aggregate at all, such as `SELECT state FROM covid GROUP BY state`, is legal but only removes duplicates, so write it the clearer way, `SELECT DISTINCT state FROM covid`.)

The same in `awk` (for reference only - I don't expect you to become `awk` masters). A group is the lec 2 awk **array** (a hash map from a string to a value: the key is the group, the value is a count, a sum or even a date), such as `n[$3]` for one counter per state, and the `END` block loops over the array to print one line per group:

```bash
#date,county,state,fips,cases,deaths
# GROUP BY is an array indexed by the group: n[$3]++ keeps one counter per state, and END prints one line per state
awk -F, 'NR>1 {n[$3]++} END {for (s in n) print s "," n[s]}' covid.csv
# ORDER BY and LIMIT are sort and head, as before
awk -F, 'NR>1 {n[$3]++} END {for (s in n) print s "," n[s]}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 5
# WHERE is the pattern, so it runs before the grouping
awk -F, '$1=="2020-12-31" {s[$3] += $5} END {for (k in s) print k "," s[k]}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 5
# AS: no equivalent, awk output has no column names (echo a header line yourself)
{ echo "state,total_cases"
  awk -F, '$1=="2020-12-31" {s[$3] += $5} END {for (k in s) print k "," s[k]}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 3
} | column -s, -t
# count(DISTINCT ...) per group: drop the repeated (state, county) pairs with sort -u first, then count
awk -F, -v OFS=, 'NR>1 {print $3, $2}' covid.csv | sort -u | awk -F, '{n[$1]++} END {for (s in n) print s "," n[s]}' | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 3
# min per group: keep the smallest date seen so far for each state
awk -F, 'NR>1 && (!($3 in m) || $1 < m[$3]) {m[$3] = $1} END {for (s in m) print s "," m[s]}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k2,2 | head -n 3
# one group per day: index the array by the date instead
awk -F, 'NR>1 {d[$1] += $6} END {for (k in d) print k "," d[k]}' covid.csv | sort -r | head -n 3
# several aggregates per group: one array per aggregate, all indexed by the state
awk -F, '$1=="2020-12-31" {n[$3]++; s[$3] += $6; if ($6 > m[$3]) m[$3] = $6} END {for (k in n) print k "," n[k] "," s[k] "," m[k]}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3nr | head -n 3
# median per group: no easy equivalent, since every value of every state must be kept and sorted
# sort by state, then by cases, and pick the middle value of each state as its last line goes by
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" {print $3, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k1,1 -k2,2n |
  awk -F, 'function out() {print prev "," (n%2 ? a[(n+1)/2] : (a[n/2] + a[n/2+1])/2)}
           $1 != prev {if (n) out(); n = 0; prev = $1} {a[++n] = $2} END {out()}' | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 3
# two grouping columns: glue them together into one array index
awk -F, 'NR>1 {k = $3 "," $2; if ($5 > m[k]) m[k] = $5} END {for (k in m) print k "," m[k]}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3nr | head -n 3
# HAVING: a test inside the END loop, after the groups are computed
awk -F, '$1=="2020-12-31" {n[$3]++} END {for (s in n) if (n[s] < 5) print s "," n[s]}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k2,2n
```

Each SQL clause has an awk counterpart:

+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| SQL                        | `awk` (and friends)                                                            |
+============================+================================================================================+
| `SELECT ...`               | `{print ...}`                                                                  |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `SELECT DISTINCT`          | `| sort -u`                                                                    |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `AS name`                  | no equivalent (no column names)                                                |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `FROM covid`               | the file name, `covid.csv`                                                     |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `WHERE ...`                | the pattern before the `{`                                                     |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY ...`             | `| sort`                                                                       |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY ... DESC`        | `| sort -r`                                                                    |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY a, b DESC`       | `| sort -k1,1 -k2,2r`                                                          |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY random()`        | `| shuf` (with `LIMIT 5`: `| shuf -n 5`)                                       |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI`    | the pattern `rand() < 0.01` (for 1%)                                           |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `LIMIT ...`                | `| head -n ...`                                                                |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `OFFSET 5`                 | `| tail -n +6`                                                                 |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `=`                        | `==`                                                                           |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `<>`                       | `!=`                                                                           |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `<` `>` `<=` `>=`          | `<` `>` `<=` `>=`                                                              |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `AND`                      | `&&`                                                                           |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `OR`                       | `||`                                                                           |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `NOT`                      | `!`                                                                            |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `LIKE 'San %'`             | `~ /^San /`                                                                    |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `LIKE '48___'`             | `~ /^48...$/`                                                                  |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `ILIKE 'dekalb'`           | `tolower($2)=="dekalb"`                                                        |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `~ '^(De|La) ?Soto$'`      | `~ /^(De|La) ?Soto$/`                                                          |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `IN ('a', 'b')`            | `($3=="a" || $3=="b")`                                                         |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `BETWEEN a AND b`          | `$1 >= a && $1 <= b`                                                           |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `IS NULL`                  | `$6==""`                                                                       |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `count(*)`                 | `{n++} END {print n}`                                                          |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `count(deaths)`            | `$6!="" {n++} END {print n}`                                                   |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `count(DISTINCT ...)`      | `| sort -u | wc -l`                                                            |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `sum(cases)`               | `{s += $5} END {print s}`                                                      |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `avg(cases)`               | `{s += $5; n++} END {print s/n}`                                               |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `round(...)`               | `printf "%.0f\n", ...`                                                         |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `max(cases)`               | `$5 > m {m = $5} END {print m}`                                                |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `min(cases)`               | `m == "" || $5 < m {m = $5} END {print m}`                                     |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `stddev(cases)`            | `sqrt((ss - s^2/n) / (n-1))`, from `s += $5; ss += $5^2; n++`                  |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `percentile_cont(0.5) ...` | `| sort -n`, then the middle line                                              |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `mode() ...`               | `| sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 1`                                      |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `GROUP BY state`           | an array indexed by the group, `n[$3]++`, printed in `END` with `for (s in n)` |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `GROUP BY state, county`   | glue the columns into one index, `n[$3 "," $2]++`                              |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| `HAVING ...`               | an `if` inside the `END` loop, `if (n[s] < 5) print ...`                       |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Remember in `awk` you refer to columns by number (which is super annoying because you have to remember that `$3` is the state), and you have to tell `sort` that column 3 holds numbers (`-k3,3n`). SQL uses the names and already knows the types. 

Which is more readable? awk or SQL? Which is faster?


A real speed-up comes next.

## Indexes

An **index** is a sorted lookup structure that the database keeps beside the table, like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find "Harris", it looks up the entry and jumps to the right pages.

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT max(cases) FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris';
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows how Postgres ran the query. Without an index you will see `Parallel Seq Scan`. This is a *sequential scan*: reading every row. There is some savings when using multiple cores. The execution time of about 53 ms. Hit "q" to return to postgres. 

Now create the index and run the same `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` again:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON covid (state, county);     -- takes about a second, once
```

In the postgres version I have installed (v18.6), the plan changes to a `Bitmap Index Scan` which uses a data structure called a "B-tree".


```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT max(cases) FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris';
```

and the time drops to **under 3 ms**. The table has 884,737 rows, and the database looked at about 300 of them.

The time to answer is now almost independent of the table's size. That is a huge advantage of databases. The index cost is paid once, when you build the index (about 1.2 seconds here), plus a little extra on every insert to keep the index up to date and some extra disk space.


Let $n$ be the number of rows in the table and $k$ the number of rows that match. The sequential scan reads all $n$ rows, so it takes $O(n)$ however small $k$ is (strictly $O(n + k)$, but $k \leq n$ so you write it as $O(n)$ since multiplicative constants drop out). The B-tree is about 3 levels deep for our 884,737 rows, and only 4 or 5 even for a billion. Finding the first match takes $O(\log n)$ steps down the tree, and the other matches sit right next to it, so a lookup takes $O(\log n + k)$:

+------------+-----------------+--------------------------------------------------------+
| Plan       | Cost            | Harris County ($n \approx 885{,}000$, $k \approx 300$) |
+============+=================+========================================================+
| Seq Scan   | $O(n)$          | about 885,000 rows read                                |
+------------+-----------------+--------------------------------------------------------+
| Index Scan | $O(\log n + k)$ | 3 tree nodes read (one per level), then 300 rows       |
+------------+-----------------+--------------------------------------------------------+

So is there a downside? So far, no: we have only *read* the table. The costs come when the data changes (every insert, update and delete must also update the index, as we will see next lecture). However, there is a small price in disk space, since the index is a second copy of the `(state, county)` columns, sorted, plus the tree above them:

```sql
-- \di+ lists the indexes with their sizes
\di+
-- the table alone, its indexes alone, and both together
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size('covid'))          AS table_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('covid'))        AS index_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('covid')) AS total;
-- 57 MB | 6344 kB | 63 MB
```

The index takes about 6 MB next to the table's 57 MB, about 11% more space. It is this small because the key repeats a lot: Harris County, Texas appears in 300 rows, and Postgres stores each repeated key only once, followed by the list of rows that have it. An index whose keys are almost all different gets no such saving: one on `(state, county, date)` takes 35 MB, more than half the size of the table. Every index you add costs its own space, so index the columns you actually search by, not every column.

 Databases in general pay for features using disk space. Note that 57MB is larger than the original 35MB covid.csv. We will see why next lecture.


### B-trees

The index Postgres builds is a **B-tree**. It is the sorted list of all the `(state, county)` keys, cut into disk pages of 8 KB, each holding a few hundred keys, plus a few levels of pages above them that say which page to open next:

```
                     [ Georgia | Ohio | Texas ]                       <- root: 1 page
                    /        |        |        \
 [Alabama ... Florida] [Georgia ... Nevada] [Ohio ... South Dakota] [Texas ... Wyoming]
          |                     |                     |                      |
   leaves: every key in sorted order, each pointing to its row in the table,
   and each leaf linked to the next one  -> -> -> ->
```

(The picture has 4 children per page; a real page has hundreds.) To find "Texas, Harris", Postgres reads the root, follows the pointer whose range contains it, and repeats one level down until it reaches a leaf: **one page read per level**. Each page narrows the search a few hundred times, not 2 times as in a binary search, so the tree is very shallow. With 300 children per page, 3 levels reach $300^3 = 27$ million keys. Then the leaves are walked left to right for as long as the key is still "Texas, Harris". That walk is also why the same index answers `<`, `BETWEEN`, `ORDER BY` and `LIKE 'San%'`: find the start, then walk. When a leaf fills up on an insert, it splits in two and the parent gets one more key, so all the leaves always stay at the same depth and no lookup is ever unlucky.


## Subqueries (nested queries)

`SELECT max(cases) FROM covid` gives the number 770915 but not the county it belongs to. You cannot just add `county` to the `SELECT`: that breaks the `GROUP BY` rule, because `max` boils all the rows down to one and Postgres would not know which county to show. The usual answer is a query inside a query, a **subquery**, in parentheses. Postgres runs the inner query first and puts its answer in its place:

```sql
-- the inner query finds 770915, and the outer one finds the row(s) with that value
SELECT date, county, state, cases FROM covid
  WHERE cases = (SELECT max(cases) FROM covid);             -- 2020-12-31 | Los Angeles | California | 770915
-- the inner query needs its own WHERE too, otherwise it finds the max of the whole country
SELECT date, county, cases FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas'
    AND cases = (SELECT max(cases) FROM covid WHERE state = 'Texas');   -- 2020-12-31 | Harris | 237727
-- any aggregate works: the counties above the national mean (6171) at the end of 2020
SELECT count(*) FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
    AND cases > (SELECT avg(cases) FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31');   -- 587 of the 3245
-- the latest day in the data, without knowing what it is
SELECT county, state, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = (SELECT max(date) FROM covid)
  ORDER BY cases DESC LIMIT 3;                              -- Los Angeles 770915, New York City 430863, Cook 393652
```

The subquery must return what its place in the outer query expects. After `=`, `<` or `>` it stands for a **single value**, so it must return exactly one row and one column, of a type that can be compared with the other side. Aggregates without `GROUP BY` always return one row, which is why they are the usual inner query. Get the shape or the type wrong and Postgres refuses:

```sql
-- many rows where one value is expected
SELECT county FROM covid
  WHERE cases = (SELECT cases FROM covid WHERE state = 'Texas');
-- ERROR:  more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression
-- two columns where one is expected
SELECT county FROM covid
  WHERE cases = (SELECT max(cases), min(cases) FROM covid);
-- ERROR:  subquery must return only one column
-- a date where a number is expected
SELECT county FROM covid
  WHERE cases = (SELECT max(date) FROM covid);
-- ERROR:  operator does not exist: integer = date
-- no rows at all is allowed: the subquery becomes NULL, and nothing equals NULL
SELECT county FROM covid
  WHERE cases = (SELECT max(cases) FROM covid WHERE state = 'Atlantis');   -- (0 rows)
```

After `IN`, the subquery stands for a **list of values** instead, so it may return many rows, but still only one column:

```sql
-- all counties in the states that have at least one county above 200,000 cases
SELECT count(*) FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
    AND state IN (SELECT state FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND cases > 200000);   -- 555
```

`ORDER BY cases DESC LIMIT 1` is the easy workaround, but it gives only one row, even when several are tied. On 2020-12-31 the fewest cases is 0, and two rows have it:

```sql
SELECT county, state, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' ORDER BY cases LIMIT 1;         -- only one of the two
SELECT county, state, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
    AND cases = (SELECT min(cases) FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31');   -- Unknown | Kansas | 0 and Unknown | Maryland | 0
```

In `awk` a subquery is a **second pass** over the file. Giving `awk` the same file twice, `covid.csv covid.csv`, reads it twice. `NR==FNR` is true only during the first file (`NR` counts all lines read so far, `FNR` only those of the current file), so the first block computes the inner answer and `next` skips the rest; the pattern after it runs on the second pass:

```bash
# the max, then the row(s) with the max
awk -F, -v OFS=, 'NR==FNR {if (FNR>1 && $5 > m) m = $5; next} FNR>1 && $5 == m {print $1, $2, $3, $5}' covid.csv covid.csv   # 2020-12-31,Los Angeles,California,770915
# the same within Texas: both passes have the Texas test
awk -F, -v OFS=, 'NR==FNR {if ($3=="Texas" && $5 > m) m = $5; next} $3=="Texas" && $5 == m {print $1, $2, $5}' covid.csv covid.csv   # 2020-12-31,Harris,237727
# above the mean: the first pass computes the mean, the second counts
awk -F, 'NR==FNR {if ($1=="2020-12-31") {s += $5; n++}; next} $1=="2020-12-31" && $5 > s/n {c++} END {print c}' covid.csv covid.csv   # 587
# the latest day: dates written YYYY-MM-DD compare correctly as text
awk -F, -v OFS=, 'NR==FNR {if (FNR>1 && $1 > d) d = $1; next} $1 == d {print $2, $3, $5}' covid.csv covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3nr | head -n 3
# the ties: sort | head -n 1 also keeps only one, the two-pass version keeps both
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" {print $2, $3, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3n | head -n 1
awk -F, -v OFS=, 'NR==FNR {if ($1=="2020-12-31" && (m == "" || $5 < m)) m = $5; next} $1=="2020-12-31" && $5 == m {print $2, $3, $5}' covid.csv covid.csv   # Unknown,Kansas,0 and Unknown,Maryland,0
```

The `awk` version reads the 35 MB file twice. Without an index Postgres also scans the table twice, but with the index on `(state, county)` both passes of the Texas query read only the 67,002 Texas rows instead of all 884,737.

## Computed columns and `CASE` logic

After `SELECT` you are not limited to column names. Any expression works: arithmetic on columns, functions, and if/else. Each one becomes a column of the answer, best named with `AS`:

```sql
-- arithmetic: careful, an integer divided by an integer is an integer in SQL, rounded down
SELECT deaths / cases FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris' AND date = '2020-12-31';   -- 0
-- make one side a decimal number first, with ::float (a "cast") or by multiplying by 100.0
SELECT deaths::float / cases FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris' AND date = '2020-12-31';   -- 0.014310532669827155
SELECT round(100.0 * deaths / cases, 2) AS death_rate FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris' AND date = '2020-12-31';   -- 1.43 (percent)
-- a computed column can be sorted by its name; the IS NOT NULL keeps the empty deaths from sorting first
SELECT county, state, round(100.0 * deaths / cases, 2) AS death_rate FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND cases >= 1000 AND deaths IS NOT NULL
  ORDER BY death_rate DESC LIMIT 3;                         -- Unknown, Puerto Rico 38.79 (most of its cases are listed by municipality, its deaths are not), Franklin, Massachusetts 7.20, New York City 5.84
-- || glues text together
SELECT county || ', ' || state AS place, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' ORDER BY cases DESC LIMIT 1;    -- Los Angeles, California | 770915
-- CASE is if/else: it turns each row into a label, which you can then group by
SELECT CASE 
  WHEN cases > 100000 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small' END 
  AS size, count(*) FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' GROUP BY size;                  -- big 16, small 3229
-- functions on dates: extract pulls out one part, here the month, which you can also group by
SELECT extract(month FROM date) AS month, count(*) FROM covid
  GROUP BY month ORDER BY month LIMIT 3;                    -- 1 39, 2 359, 3 23482: the rows grow as the virus spreads
```

`awk` does the same with arithmetic on fields, the `? :` operator for if/else, and string functions. There are no integer surprises: `awk` always divides as decimals.

```bash
# arithmetic on fields, rounded by printf
awk -F, '$3=="Texas" && $2=="Harris" && $1=="2020-12-31" {printf "%.2f\n", 100 * $6 / $5}' covid.csv   # 1.43
# the computed column, then sort by it
awk -F, '$1=="2020-12-31" && $5 >= 1000 && $6 != "" {printf "%s,%s,%.2f\n", $2, $3, 100 * $6 / $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3nr | head -n 3
# gluing text: put the pieces next to each other
awk -F, '$1=="2020-12-31" {print $2 ", " $3 "," $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3nr | head -n 1   # Los Angeles, California,770915
# CASE is the ? : operator (condition ? if true : if false), then group by the label
awk -F, '$1=="2020-12-31" {size = ($5 > 100000 ? "big" : "small"); n[size]++} END {for (s in n) print s "," n[s]}' covid.csv   # big,16 and small,3229
# extract(month ...): substr cuts characters 6 and 7 out of YYYY-MM-DD, and + 0 turns "03" into 3
awk -F, 'NR>1 {n[substr($1, 6, 2) + 0]++} END {for (m in n) print m "," n[m]}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k1,1n | head -n 3   # 1,39 2,359 3,23482
```

## Set operations: `UNION`, `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT`

These combine the answers of two whole queries, treating each answer as a set of rows. Both queries must return the same number of columns, with matching types, and the result has no repeated rows:

* `A UNION B`: the rows in either answer
* `A INTERSECT B`: the rows in both
* `A EXCEPT B`: the rows in `A` but not in `B`
* `A UNION ALL B`: both answers one after the other, repeats kept (and faster, since there is nothing to check)

```sql
-- the counties with a row in March but none in December: all 18 are "Unknown", cases that were later assigned to a real county
SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date BETWEEN '2020-03-01' AND '2020-03-31'
EXCEPT
SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date BETWEEN '2020-12-01' AND '2020-12-31'
ORDER BY state, county;                                     -- Arizona Unknown, California Unknown, ... (18 rows)
-- the other way round: counties with no row yet in March, mostly the virus reaching them later
SELECT count(*) FROM (
  SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date BETWEEN '2020-12-01' AND '2020-12-31'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date BETWEEN '2020-03-01' AND '2020-03-31'
) t;                                                        -- 1104
-- counties among the first to report (data on 2020-01-31) and among the biggest at the end of the year
SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-01-31'
INTERSECT
SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND cases > 200000;   -- Arizona Maricopa, California Los Angeles, Illinois Cook
-- either one: 6 + 6 counties, but the 3 above are in both, so 9 rows
SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-01-31'
UNION
SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND cases > 200000;   -- 9 rows
-- UNION ALL keeps the repeats: 12 rows
SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-01-31'
UNION ALL
SELECT state, county FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND cases > 200000;   -- 12 rows
```

The `ORDER BY` at the end sorts the combined answer, not just the second query.

In the shell, these are `comm` (which compares two *sorted* files line by line) and `sort -u`. `comm -12` prints the lines in both files, `-23` those only in the first and `-13` those only in the second. `<( ... )` hands the output of a command to `comm` as if it were a file:

```bash
# EXCEPT: lines only in the first list
comm -23 <(awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1 >= "2020-03-01" && $1 <= "2020-03-31" {print $3, $2}' covid.csv | sort -u) \
         <(awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1 >= "2020-12-01" && $1 <= "2020-12-31" {print $3, $2}' covid.csv | sort -u)
# INTERSECT: lines in both lists
comm -12 <(awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-01-31" {print $3, $2}' covid.csv | sort -u) \
         <(awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" && $5 > 200000 {print $3, $2}' covid.csv | sort -u)
# UNION: both lists together, with the repeats removed
{ awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-01-31" {print $3, $2}' covid.csv
  awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" && $5 > 200000 {print $3, $2}' covid.csv; } | sort -u
# UNION ALL: both lists together, as they are
{ awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-01-31" {print $3, $2}' covid.csv
  awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" && $5 > 200000 {print $3, $2}' covid.csv; }
```

## Window functions

An aggregate with `GROUP BY` boils each group down to one row. A **window function** computes the same kind of per-group answer but *keeps every row*, and writes the answer next to it. The group is called the **window** and is given after `OVER`: `PARTITION BY` says which rows belong together (like `GROUP BY`), and `ORDER BY` says in which order to go through them. Window functions are standard SQL and work in almost every database (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB, BigQuery, Spark).

The classic use is the **top row per group**, such as each state's biggest county. `GROUP BY state` cannot do it, for the same reason as `max(cases)` in the subquery section: it finds the biggest number but not the county it belongs to. `row_number()` numbers the rows of each state from 1, biggest first, and then we keep the 1s:

```sql
-- the window function can't go in WHERE (WHERE runs before it is computed), so it goes in a subquery in FROM
SELECT state, county, cases FROM (
  SELECT state, county, cases,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY cases DESC) AS r
  FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
) t
WHERE r = 1 ORDER BY state LIMIT 3;                         -- Alabama Jefferson 52339, Alaska Anchorage 22820, Arizona Maricopa 322449
-- the top 3 per state is just r <= 3, which GROUP BY can't do at all
SELECT county, cases, r FROM (
  SELECT state, county, cases,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY cases DESC) AS r
  FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
) t
WHERE state = 'Texas' AND r <= 3 ORDER BY r;                -- Harris 237727 1, Dallas 193318 2, Tarrant 150004 3
-- rank() gives tied rows the same number, then skips: here 1, 1, 3, 3 (row_number would give 1, 2, 3, 4)
-- with no PARTITION BY the window is the whole answer
SELECT state, county, cases, rank() OVER (ORDER BY cases) AS r FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' ORDER BY cases LIMIT 4;         -- Kansas/Maryland Unknown 0 1, Hawaii Kalawao 1 3, Maine Unknown 1 3
-- an aggregate with OVER: each county next to the total of its state, and its share of it
SELECT county, cases,
       round(100.0 * cases / sum(cases) OVER (PARTITION BY state), 1) AS pct_of_state
  FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND state = 'Texas'
  ORDER BY cases DESC LIMIT 3;                              -- Harris 13.4%, Dallas 10.9%, Tarrant 8.5%
-- lag() looks at the previous row of the window. cases is a running total, so today minus yesterday = the new cases
SELECT date, cases, cases - lag(cases) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS new_cases FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris'
  ORDER BY date DESC LIMIT 3;                               -- 2020-12-31 237727 1054, 2020-12-30 236673 1937, 2020-12-29 234736 1406
-- the same for every county at once: PARTITION BY restarts lag() at each county
SELECT county, state, new_cases FROM (
  SELECT county, state, date,
         cases - lag(cases) OVER (PARTITION BY state, county ORDER BY date) AS new_cases
  FROM covid
) t
WHERE date = '2020-12-31' ORDER BY new_cases DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 3;   -- Los Angeles 14503, Maricopa 5181, New York City 4584
```

Postgres also has a shortcut for the top row per group, `SELECT DISTINCT ON (state) state, county, cases FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31' ORDER BY state, cases DESC`, but it works only in Postgres and keeps just one of several tied rows. Window functions work everywhere and let you choose how to treat ties.

They have a cost. A window function must **sort** the rows of each window, which is $O(n \log n)$. For one day (3,245 rows) that is cheap, about 26 ms here. For the latest row of every county over the whole table (884,737 rows) it took about 1.5 s, while a `GROUP BY` version (`max(date)` per county, then an `IN` subquery to find those rows) took about 0.3 s, because a `GROUP BY` can use a hash table, which needs no sort.

In `awk` a window is "sort by the group, then walk down the lines remembering the previous one". The `sort` does what `PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY` does:

```bash
# row_number() = 1: sort by state, then cases from biggest, and keep the first line of each state
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" {print $3, $2, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k1,1 -k3,3nr | awk -F, '!seen[$1]++' | head -n 3
# row_number(): NR after the sort is the row number
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" && $3=="Texas" {print $2, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k2,2nr | awk -v OFS=, '{print $0, NR}' | head -n 3
# rank(): the line number of the first line with this value
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" {print $3, $2, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3n | awk -F, -v OFS=, '{if (NR == 1 || $3 != prev) r = NR; prev = $3; print $0, r}' | head -n 4
# sum() OVER (PARTITION BY state): a first pass for the total, as for subqueries
awk -F, 'NR==FNR {if ($1=="2020-12-31" && $3=="Texas") s += $5; next} $1=="2020-12-31" && $3=="Texas" {printf "%s,%d,%.1f\n", $2, $5, 100 * $5 / s}' covid.csv covid.csv | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 3
# lag(): remember the previous line's value
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$3=="Texas" && $2=="Harris" {print $1, $5}' covid.csv | sort | awk -F, -v OFS=, '{print $1, $2, (NR > 1 ? $2 - prev : ""); prev = $2}' | tail -n 3
# lag() with PARTITION BY: also remember the previous line's county, and only subtract within the same one
awk -F, -v OFS=, 'NR>1 {print $3, $2, $1, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k1,1 -k2,2 -k3,3 | awk -F, -v OFS=, '{k = $1 "," $2; if (k == pk && $3 == "2020-12-31") print $2, $1, $4 - prev; pk = k; prev = $4}' | sort -t, -k3,3nr | head -n 3
```


## `WITH`: naming a subquery

Subqueries in `FROM`, like the window function queries above, get hard to read as they nest. (A subquery in `FROM`, the `( ... ) t` in those queries, is called a **derived table**.) `WITH` lets you write the inner query first and give it a name, a **common table expression** (CTE). After that, the name works like a table, for this one query only:

```sql
-- the top county per state from the window function section, written with WITH: read it top to bottom
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT state, county, cases,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY cases DESC) AS r
  FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
)
SELECT state, county, cases FROM ranked
  WHERE r = 1 ORDER BY state LIMIT 3;                       -- Alabama Jefferson 52339, Alaska Anchorage 22820, Arizona Maricopa 322449
-- a name can be used more than once: here in the outer query and in its subquery, so the date is written only once
WITH dec31 AS (SELECT * FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31')
SELECT count(*) FROM dec31
  WHERE cases > (SELECT avg(cases) FROM dec31);             -- 587, as in the subquery section
-- names can build on each other, separated by commas: national totals per day, then the new cases per day
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT date, sum(cases) AS cases FROM covid GROUP BY date
),
new AS (
  SELECT date, cases - lag(cases) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS new_cases FROM daily
)
SELECT date, new_cases FROM new
  ORDER BY new_cases DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 3;               -- 2020-12-11 280016, 2020-12-18 251190, 2020-12-16 244827
-- a window can also be a range of rows around the current one: the 7-day moving average of the new cases
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT date, sum(cases) AS cases FROM covid GROUP BY date
),
new AS (
  SELECT date, cases - lag(cases) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS new_cases FROM daily
)
SELECT date, new_cases,
       round(avg(new_cases) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)) AS week_avg
  FROM new ORDER BY date DESC LIMIT 2;                      -- 2020-12-31 231024 188556, 2020-12-30 228949 183197
```

The third query needs `NULLS LAST` because `lag()` has no previous row on the first day, so that day's `new_cases` is `NULL`, and `DESC` would sort it first. In the same way, `sum(new_cases) OVER (ORDER BY date)` (no `ROWS ...`) is a **running total**: the sum of all rows up to the current one.

In the shell, the closest thing to a CTE is saving an intermediate result to a file, for example `awk -F, '$1=="2020-12-31"' covid.csv > dec31.csv`, and then using `dec31.csv` in the next commands. Pipes play the role of names that build on each other:

```bash
# daily: national totals per day; then new: the change from the previous day (lag)
awk -F, 'NR>1 {d[$1] += $5} END {for (k in d) print k "," d[k]}' covid.csv | sort |
  awk -F, -v OFS=, 'NR > 1 {print $1, $2 - prev} {prev = $2}' | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 3   # 2020-12-11,280016 ...
# the 7-day moving average: keep the last 7 new counts in an array, w[NR % 7], and average them
awk -F, 'NR>1 {d[$1] += $5} END {for (k in d) print k "," d[k]}' covid.csv | sort |
  awk -F, 'NR > 1 {new = $2 - prev; w[NR % 7] = new; n = (NR - 1 < 7 ? NR - 1 : 7); s = 0; for (i in w) s += w[i]; printf "%s,%d,%.0f\n", $1, new, s / n} {prev = $2}' | tail -n 2   # 2020-12-30,228949,183197 and 2020-12-31,231024,188556
```

## Changing the data: `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE`

All the queries so far only *read*. Three more commands change the rows. Let's try them on a copy, so `covid` itself stays as it is. `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` saves the answer of any query as a new table:

```sql
-- a new table holding the Texas rows (it is a real copy: later changes to covid do not reach it)
CREATE TABLE texas AS SELECT * FROM covid WHERE state = 'Texas';   -- SELECT 67002
-- INSERT adds rows; the values go in the order of the columns
INSERT INTO texas VALUES ('2021-01-01', 'Harris', 'Texas', '48201', 239000, 3500);   -- INSERT 0 1
-- or name the columns you give; the ones you leave out become NULL
INSERT INTO texas (date, county, state, cases) VALUES ('2021-01-01', 'Dallas', 'Texas', 195000);   -- INSERT 0 1
SELECT * FROM texas WHERE date = '2021-01-01';              -- the two new rows, Dallas with no fips and no deaths
-- UPDATE changes the columns after SET, in every row its WHERE matches
UPDATE texas SET deaths = 2400
  WHERE county = 'Dallas' AND date = '2021-01-01';          -- UPDATE 1
UPDATE texas SET county = 'Harris County'
  WHERE county = 'Harris';                                  -- UPDATE 303: one command, every matching row
-- DELETE removes every row its WHERE matches
DELETE FROM texas WHERE date = '2021-01-01';                -- DELETE 2
DELETE FROM texas WHERE county = 'Unknown';                 -- DELETE 1
SELECT count(*) FROM texas;                                 -- 67001
-- DROP TABLE removes the whole table
DROP TABLE texas;
```

After each command `psql` reports how many rows it touched (`UPDATE 303`, `DELETE 2`). Read that number every time. It is your only check that the `WHERE` matched what you meant.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `UPDATE` and `DELETE` without `WHERE`
`DELETE FROM texas;` deletes *every* row, and `UPDATE texas SET deaths = 0;` changes every row, with no question asked and no undo. Before you run one, run the same `WHERE` as a `SELECT count(*)` first, and check the number.
:::

Compare this with Lab 3, Part 5: adding or deleting a single row of a Parquet file meant reading and rewriting the whole file. Here each command touches only the rows it names.

### Changing the table itself: `ALTER TABLE`

`INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` change the rows. `ALTER TABLE` changes the *table*: its columns, their names and their types. Again on a copy, here of the whole table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE covid_copy AS SELECT * FROM covid;                          -- SELECT 884737
\timing on
-- ADD COLUMN: every existing row gets NULL in the new column
ALTER TABLE covid_copy ADD COLUMN notes text;                             -- about 2 ms
-- or a DEFAULT value instead of NULL, also in about 2 ms
ALTER TABLE covid_copy ADD COLUMN reviewed boolean DEFAULT false;
-- a new column is usually filled in with UPDATE
ALTER TABLE covid_copy ADD COLUMN death_rate double precision;
UPDATE covid_copy SET death_rate = deaths::float / cases WHERE cases > 0; -- UPDATE 884022, about 2 s: every row is rewritten
-- RENAME COLUMN and DROP COLUMN
ALTER TABLE covid_copy RENAME COLUMN death_rate TO cfr;                   -- about 2 ms
ALTER TABLE covid_copy DROP COLUMN notes;                                 -- about 2 ms
-- ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE: a bigger type, for when cases might pass 2 billion
ALTER TABLE covid_copy ALTER COLUMN cases TYPE bigint;                    -- about 1.3 s
-- text to integer has no automatic conversion
ALTER TABLE covid_copy ALTER COLUMN fips TYPE integer;
-- ERROR:  column "fips" cannot be cast automatically to type integer
-- HINT:  You might need to specify "USING fips::integer".
-- (USING fips::integer would work, but would turn '01001' into 1001: this is why fips is text)
-- RENAME TO renames the table itself
ALTER TABLE covid_copy RENAME TO covid_scratch;
\timing off
\d covid_scratch
DROP TABLE covid_scratch;
```

Adding, renaming or dropping a column takes a few milliseconds whatever the size of the table, because Postgres only changes its description of the table (what `\d` prints). It does not touch the rows. A dropped column is just hidden, and its space is reclaimed later as the rows are rewritten. Changing a column's type is different: every value must be converted, so the whole table is rewritten, and it takes about as long as the `UPDATE` does.

Compare this with Parquet. A Parquet file stores each column separately, but its metadata and row groups are written once, so even adding a column means writing a new file. With a table split over thousands of Parquet files, adding one column means rewriting every one of them.

## Views: naming a query for good

A CTE's name lasts for one query. A **view** is a named query *saved in the database*: every later query, in any session, from `psql`, R or Python, can use it like a table, until you remove it.

```sql
-- the dec31 CTE from above, saved once
CREATE VIEW dec31 AS SELECT * FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31';
-- now it works in any query, without repeating the WITH
SELECT count(*) FROM dec31;                                 -- 3245
SELECT county, cases FROM dec31
  WHERE state = 'Texas' ORDER BY cases DESC LIMIT 1;        -- Harris 237727
-- \d+ shows the saved query behind it
\d+ dec31
```

A view stores **no data**. It is only the saved `SELECT`, and every query against the view runs it again. So the view is always current. Change a row of `covid` with `UPDATE` and the view shows the change at once:

```sql
UPDATE covid SET cases = cases + 1
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris' AND date = '2020-12-31';
SELECT county, cases FROM dec31
  WHERE state = 'Texas' ORDER BY cases DESC LIMIT 1;        -- Harris 237728
-- put it back
UPDATE covid SET cases = cases - 1
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris' AND date = '2020-12-31';
```

A **materialized view** does store the answer, like a table. Reading it is fast, but it does not see later changes until you refresh it:

```sql
CREATE VIEW daily AS
  SELECT date, sum(cases) AS cases FROM covid GROUP BY date;
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_m AS
  SELECT date, sum(cases) AS cases FROM covid GROUP BY date;
\timing on
SELECT max(cases) FROM daily;                               -- 20024801, about 70 ms: the GROUP BY runs again
SELECT max(cases) FROM daily_m;                             -- 20024801, under 1 ms: it only reads the 346 saved rows
-- after an UPDATE to covid, daily is current at once, but daily_m is out of date until
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_m;                          -- runs the query again and saves the new answer
\timing off
```

Views are used everywhere in practice:

* **Data warehouses and analytics teams.** The most popular modern tool for analytics pipelines, **dbt**, is largely a system for writing `SELECT` statements that it saves as views or tables. Analysts at many companies spend their days building views on top of views: raw data, then cleaned, then business-ready.
* **Dashboards and BI tools.** Tableau, Power BI, Looker and Metabase are usually pointed at views, not raw tables, so the logic sits in one place in the database instead of being copied into every report.
* **A stable name to hand to others.** R, Python or a colleague can query `dec31` without knowing how it is built.
* **Security.** "Analysts may see these columns, or only their region's rows" is very often enforced by giving people access to a view instead of the table, for example `CREATE VIEW patients_public AS SELECT visit_date, age FROM patients`, which leaves out `name` (Lab 3, scenario (b)). Giving the access itself is done with `GRANT`, for a later lecture.
* **Keeping old code working.** When a table is restructured, a view with the old name and shape lets existing queries keep running.
* **Materialized views** are the standard fix when a dashboard query is too slow to run on every page load.

They also have their usual problems:

* **Hidden cost.** A view looks like a cheap table, but every query re-runs it. Views built on views built on views can hide a slow query several layers down.
* **They lock the tables underneath.** You often cannot change a column while a view uses it:

```sql
ALTER TABLE covid ALTER COLUMN cases TYPE bigint;
-- ERROR:  cannot alter type of a column used by a view or rule
-- DETAIL:  rule _RETURN on view dec31 depends on column "cases"
```

The shell has no real equivalent. The closest to a view is a saved script (or a shell function), which runs the whole pipeline again every time you call it and so is always current. A file you wrote once, such as `awk -F, '$1=="2020-12-31"' covid.csv > dec31.csv`, is like a materialized view: fast to read, but stale as soon as `covid.csv` changes.

Clean up:

```sql
DROP VIEW dec31;
DROP VIEW daily;
DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_m;
```




## The database checks your data

Try to add a row with a nonsense value:

```sql
INSERT INTO covid VALUES ('2021-01-01', 'Harris', 'Texas', '48201', 'N/A', 0);
-- ERROR:  invalid input syntax for type integer: "N/A"
```

A CSV would have accepted that line without complaint, and the problem would have appeared much later, in the middle of an analysis. A database refuses bad data at the door. Types are the simplest of its guarantees. Later you can add rules such as `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE` and `CHECK`.

## Changing data

Fixing one value touches only the rows you name:

```sql
UPDATE covid SET deaths = deaths + 1
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris' AND date = '2020-12-31';
```

A database does not care where a row "goes": it writes the change into free space and updates its index, which takes a fraction of a millisecond. Compare that with rewriting a 35 GB Parquet file. You can also wrap several changes in a **transaction** (`BEGIN; ... COMMIT;`), and either all of them happen or none of them do. If the machine crashes halfway through, the database recovers to a consistent state.



## What did you install?

Postgres is a lot of software. Add it up, with `du` ("disk usage") for the program files and the database itself for your data:

```bash
du -ch /usr/lib/postgresql /usr/share/postgresql | tail -n 1   # the program
psql -At -c "SELECT pg_size_pretty(sum(pg_database_size(datname)))
             FROM pg_database"                          # all your data
```

`du -c` adds a grand total at the end and `tail -n 1` keeps only that line. On Ubuntu the program is about 50 MB. (On a Mac with Homebrew, use `du -shL "$(brew --prefix postgresql@18)"`.) The `covid` table alone took about 63 MB with its index, almost twice the 35 MB CSV.

That is a lot of space for a program whose job is to store rows. But look at what it bought you in this unit:

- **Speed:** the same question went from scanning every row (about 70 ms here, and growing with the table) to under 1 ms with an index, and that stays true as the table grows.
- **Correctness:** typed columns refused `'N/A'` as a number, and rules such as `NOT NULL` and `UNIQUE` can refuse other nonsense when it arrives.
- **Safe changes:** single-row updates and transactions that happen completely or not at all, even if the machine crashes.
- **Many users at once:** many programs reading and writing the same tables at once without corrupting them.
- **A query language** instead of one-off shell pipelines: SQL, with joins, grouping and sorting, and a planner that picks how to run each query.

PostgreSQL grew out of research at Berkeley in the 1980s and has had decades of engineering since. Nobody would write all of that again for one analysis. That is why it is worth the space: you get it for free, and it is already installed.

## Why is the table bigger than the CSV?

The `covid` table alone is 57 MB, bigger than the CSV and far bigger than the Parquet file of Lecture 3. Postgres stores each row in a way built for *changing* it, while Parquet is built for *storing* it compactly:

+----------------+----------+----------------+
| Format         | Size     | Per row        |
+================+==========+================+
| CSV            | 35.9 MB  | about 40 bytes |
+----------------+----------+----------------+
| Parquet (zstd) | ~3.3 MB  | about 4 bytes  |
+----------------+----------+----------------+
| Postgres table | 57 MB    | about 67 bytes |
+----------------+----------+----------------+

Postgres is bigger than the CSV because of overhead that every row pays:

* **A row header of about 24 bytes.** It holds the ID of the transaction that created the row and of the one that deleted it (`xmin` and `xmax`), plus some flags. That is how Postgres lets many people read and write at once, and how it undoes a failed transaction: each reader checks those IDs to decide whether it should see the row.
* **A 4-byte pointer to each row**, stored at the top of its page.
* **Padding.** Values are aligned to 4- or 8-byte boundaries, so some bytes between columns sit empty.

That is about 28 bytes per row before any data, or roughly 25 MB of the 57. The data itself is actually *smaller* than in the CSV: a date takes 4 bytes instead of 10 characters, and `cases` takes 4 bytes instead of up to 6 digits. The overhead outweighs that saving.

Parquet is so much smaller for three reasons:

* **Columns, not rows.** All 884,737 states sit next to each other, so dictionary encoding stores "Texas" once plus a small code per row (Lecture 3).
* **Compression.** zstd squeezes the already-encoded columns further. Postgres does not compress ordinary rows at all; it only compresses single values larger than about 2 KB.
* **No per-row overhead.** No header, no pointer, no padding.

So the 57 MB is the price of the database's features. The row header is what lets `UPDATE` change one row without rewriting the file, and what lets a transaction happen fully or not at all. Parquet has none of that, which is exactly the pain you felt in Lab 3, Part 5: adding one row rewrites the whole file.

## Clean up

```bash
dropdb lec04                     # delete the whole database
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it
1. Find the five counties with the highest `deaths` on 2020-12-31, as a single SQL statement (`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`). Your first attempt will probably list counties with *no* number at all. Some rows in the CSV have an empty `deaths`, which the database stores as `NULL`, and `ORDER BY ... DESC` puts `NULL` first. Fix it with `NULLS LAST`.
2. Time the query "maximum `cases` in Harris, Texas" with and without the index (`DROP INDEX` to remove it). Then do the same with `awk` on the CSV. How many times faster is the indexed query?
3. Load the CSV again into a second table, but declare `cases` as `text`. What changes, and which of the queries above breaks or gives wrong answers? (Try `max(cases)`: as text, `'9999'` sorts after `'237727'`.)
:::





## Other topics

2. Constraints and the primary key: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK (cases >= 0), DEFAULT and especially PRIMARY KEY. lec05's "The database checks your data" only names them. A primary key on (date, state, county) would show both refusing duplicate rows and getting an index for free. You'll also need it for joins later, since a foreign key points at a primary key.
3. NULL helpers: coalesce(deaths, 0) replaces a NULL with a default, and NULLIF(cases, 0) avoids dividing by zero. The death-rate query would fail with "division by zero" on any county with 0 cases if the cases >= 1000 filter were removed. Students will hit both in practice.
5. Date arithmetic: date - 7, date - interval '1 month', date_trunc('week', date), current_date. We have extract but not arithmetic or truncation, which are what grouping by week or month really need.

Smaller things, one line each:
- String functions: lower, upper, length, substr, trim.
- INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ("upsert": insert, or update if the row already exists). It needs a UNIQUE constraint or primary key, so it belongs after point 2.
- RETURNING: DELETE ... RETURNING * shows the rows that were just removed.
- TRUNCATE: empty a table instantly, keeping its definition.
- FETCH FIRST 1 ROWS WITH TIES: the standard way to get top-N rows with ties. That's a cleaner answer to the tie problem in the subquery section.
- Quoted identifiers: "Column Name" for columns with spaces or capitals, which come up when loading CSVs made by others.
